reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: There is complete anatomical discontinuity between the ascending and descending aorta, so the lower body depends on flow through the arterial duct
Types are classified by the site of interruption relative to the arch vessels, with interruption distal to the left subclavian, between the left carotid and subclavian, or between the carotids
The systemic circulation to the lower body is duct-dependent, and closure of the duct precipitates shock, acidosis and collapse
It almost always coexists with a ventricular septal defect, and a subaortic narrowing is common
Prostaglandin infusion to maintain ductal patency is life-saving while the neonate is stabilised and prepared for surgery
Type B interruption is strongly associated with 22q11.2 deletion and the DiGeorge phenotype
Definitive treatment is surgical reconstruction re-establishing arch continuity and repairing associated defects
reference.pathophysiology: Interrupted aortic arch is an extreme conotruncal and arch anomaly in which a segment of the aortic arch is absent, leaving no luminal continuity between the proximal and distal aorta. Perfusion of the lower body and any arch vessels beyond the interruption depends entirely on right-to-left flow through the arterial duct. While the duct remains open the circulation is balanced, but as the duct constricts after birth lower-body perfusion falls abruptly, causing profound metabolic acidosis, renal and gut hypoperfusion and cardiovascular collapse. An almost invariable ventricular septal defect and frequent posterior malalignment causing subaortic obstruction shape the intracardiac haemodynamics and pulmonary overcirculation. The lesion, particularly type B, is closely linked to 22q11.2 microdeletion.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis or metabolic disease causing neonatal collapse
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography to confirm arch discontinuity, the ventricular septal defect and subaortic anatomy
Cardiac CT or MR angiography to define the interruption site and arch vessels
Preductal and postductal saturation and blood pressure comparison
Genetic testing for 22q11.2 deletion with calcium and immune assessment
Arterial blood gas to detect metabolic acidosis from lower-body hypoperfusion
Cardiac catheterisation in selected complex cases
redFlags: Circulatory collapse and severe acidosis as the duct closes
Absent or weak lower-limb pulses with differential upper and lower body perfusion
Oliguria or signs of gut ischaemia from lower-body hypoperfusion
Hypocalcaemia and immune deficiency in the DiGeorge spectrum
reference.prognosis: Untreated the condition is rapidly fatal once the duct closes, but with prostaglandin stabilisation and surgical repair survival is good, although recurrent arch obstruction and residual subaortic stenosis may require reintervention.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing neonatal collapse as sepsis and missing the duct-dependent lesion
Allowing the duct to close before prostaglandin is started
Overlooking subaortic obstruction that complicates surgical planning
Failing to test for 22q11.2 deletion, with its calcium, immune and irradiated blood product implications
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
